title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response — Compliance Evidence Workflows
author: Priya Nair
body:
Purpose and scope:
This document defines Redwood Inference’s end-to-end security and compliance controls for: role-based access control (RBAC) and authentication; audit logging and log integrity; data residency and retention policies; Secure Software Development Life Cycle (Secure SDLC) requirements; incident response security procedures with forensic evidence capture; compliance evidence workflows; and risk/exception request processes.

Audience:
Security engineers, platform/infra engineers, compliance owners, service owners, product leads, and auditors.

Owners and responsibilities:
- Security (team): policy owner, controls design, evidence review, exception approvals.
- Eng-Infra: IAM implementation, logging pipeline, KMS and cross-region key management.
- Eng-SRE: alerting, runbooks, incident response coordination, log retention enforcement.
- Service owners: maintain access lists, attestations, and service-specific proofs.
- Compliance (GRC): evidence collection, SOC2/ISO audit readiness.

1) RBAC & Authentication (Design and operational rules)
Summary:
Redwood enforces centralized RBAC backed by SSO (Okta) and SCIM provisioning into GitHub, Terraform Cloud, cloud IAM groups, and Datadog/Splunk. Principle of least privilege and role separation are mandatory.

Core roles (examples):
- org-admin (very limited; mostly founders/execs) — organization-wide visibility, emergency actions.
- security-admin — manage security config, policies, evidence access.
- infra-admin — deploy infra, manage cloud accounts (limited scope per-project).
- service-owner — own runtime services, approve read/write grants for their service.
- developer — code & CI access, ephemeral dev env access.
- support / analyst — read-only telemetry and logs scoped to customer products.
- svc-account (machine identity) — scoped API keys with expiration and owner.

Authentication and session controls:
- Primary IdP: Okta SAML/SCIM; MFA (Okta Verify or hardware token) is required for all human accounts.
- Session duration: default 8h for interactive SSO; 12h max for elevated console sessions requiring reauthentication.
- Service principals: use ephemeral short-lived credentials (AWS STS) via HashiCorp Vault where possible. Long-lived keys are disallowed unless reviewed and approved.
- SCIM provisioning required for all team-role assignments; manual adds to high-priv groups require 2 approvers (security + manager).

Provisioning procedure (numbered):
1. Request via internal access request form (Jira ticket tagged ACCESS).
2. Owner (service or infra) reviews and confirms least privilege.
3. Security approves for high-priv groups (security-admin, infra-admin, org-admin).
4. SCIM provisioning runs and access is time-bound (default 90 days auto-expiry).

Periodic attestation:
- Quarterly attestation emails from service-owners prompting revalidation; remediation window 14 days.

2) Audit logging (events, pipeline, integrity checks)
What we log:
- Authentication events: SSO logins, MFA failures, session revocations (Okta).
- Authorization changes: RBAC grants/revocations, IAM policy changes, SCIM group changes.
- Administrative actions: KMS key rotations, Vault policy changes, org-admin actions.
- Deployment and pipeline events: GitHub actions privileged runs, Terraform Cloud plan/apply, image promotions.
- Runtime security events: container restarts, privilege escalations, suspicious API patterns (rate spikes), data exfil patterns.

Logging pipeline and storage:
- Agents publish logs to a central ingestion layer: Fluentd/Vector -> Kinesis (us-east-1) -> S3 buckets per-region -> archival to Glacier after retention window -> streaming to Splunk (security) and Datadog (ops/alerts).
- Audit logs (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Okta logs) are forwarded to dedicated audit S3 buckets with object lock enabled for high-sensitivity retention where required.

SLOs and monitoring:
- Ingestion latency: 95th percentile <= 2 minutes from event -> central ingestion.
- Availability: audit search APIs (Splunk/Datadog) 99.9% monthly.
- Integrity checks: daily signed manifest of new audit objects (SHA256) validated by the security team. Failures auto-open incident ticket.

Audit event retention matrix (table):
- "event_type | default_retention | archival | owner"
- "authentication | 1 year | Glacier after 1y | security"
- "authorizations | 7 years (for customer-sensitive) / 3 years default | Glacier after 7y | security/compliance"
- "deployment/pipeline | 1 year | Delete after 1y unless evidence | eng-infra"
- "runtime-telemetry | 90 days | reduced-resolution aggregated storage after 90d | eng-sre"

Regional & data residency considerations:
- Logs generated in EU customer workloads are stored in EU S3 buckets (eu-west-1 or customer-specified region) and never exit the region unless explicit cross-border transfer consent is recorded.
- Keys: use regional AWS KMS keys for region-locked data; cross-region key usage requires documented exception and dual-approval.

3) Data residency & retention policies
Default retention windows (applies to company telemetry and platform logs):
- Internal audit logs (authentication, authorizations): 3 years default; 7 years where required for compliance (SOC2/ISO/Customer contract).
- Customer payload metadata (non-PII): 90 days default; can be customized per contract.
- Customer data (including content): handled according to customer contract; default hosted offering does not persist user content beyond configured retention window and cache TTLs.

Encryption & key management:
- All stored audit logs and customer data at rest must be encrypted with AWS KMS CMKs.
- Secrets: HashiCorp Vault for runtime secrets with automatic lease/renewal. Access to Vault audit logs restricted to security+service-owner.

Data deletion & proof of deletion:
- Deletion requests (customer or legal) follow the Data Deletion Runbook: issue deletion job, empty S3 objects removed, object lifecycle ensures permanent deletion after 24 hours, and a signed deletion manifest is produced as evidence.
- For cross-region deletion, the runbook includes verification steps and time-stamped manifests copied to the compliance evidence bucket.

4) Secure SDLC (gates and controls)
Pipeline controls:
- Code hosting: GitHub with branch protection and required reviews (2 reviewers for service code; 1 security review for changes touching auth/crypto or infra-as-code).
- Dependency management: Dependabot daily; Snyk or equivalent vulnerability scan on pull request and weekly baseline scans. Critical vulnerabilities (CVSS >= 9) must be remediated or mitigated within 72 hours.
- Static analysis: SonarQube/SAST runs on PR; fail build on high severity findings unless documented exception.
- Secrets scanning: Pre-commit and CI checks to block secrets in commits.

Release requirements:
- All production deploys must have: (1) successful CI (unit/integration), (2) canary config (minimum 1% traffic for 30 minutes), (3) rollback playbook in GitHub release notes.
- Infrastructure changes require Terraform plan approval, drift checks, and a post-deploy verification checklist owned by Eng-SRE.

Developer onboarding & training:
- Annual secure-coding training required for engineers; new hires complete a 2-week security checklist.

5) Incident response — security procedures and evidence collection
Detection & triage:
- Alerts route to Datadog -> PagerDuty escalation (security on-call). All security incidents trigger a P1/P2 triage as defined in the Incident Response Runbook.

Initial containment checklist (first 60 minutes):
1. Triage and classify incident type (data exposure, privilege compromise, infrastructure compromise).
2. Collect volatile evidence (memory snapshots, live container processes) and record timestamps. Use approved forensic tooling (GRR, Volatility) where applicable.
3. Rotate affected credentials and revoke compromised sessions (Okta session revocation, AWS STS token revocation).
4. Isolate impacted hosts or services (network ACLs, security groups).

Evidence capture & chain of custody:
- Evidence artifacts include logs (raw and processed), memory images, disk snapshots, network captures (pcap), affected Git commits, and pipeline run artifacts.
- All artifacts are tagged with incident ID and stored in the incident evidence bucket (s3://redwood-incidents/<incident-id>/) with object-lock enabled.
- Chain of custody document must be completed by the on-call investigator and attached to the incident ticket with signatures from the investigator and security lead.

Forensics & post-incident analysis:
- Forensic timeline: initial capture within 4 hours, preliminary analysis within 48 hours, full report within 14 business days.
- Post-incident remediation tracked via a follow-up Jira epic with owners, rollback steps, compensating controls, and verification tests.

Customer and legal notifications:
- Notification timelines align with contractual SLAs and legal requirements: initial customer notification within 72 hours for confirmed customer-impacting data exposures unless legally prohibited.

6) Compliance evidence workflows (SOC2 / ISO / customer audits)
Evidence sources and canonical storage:
- Canonical evidence store: Confluence pages + a read-only evidence S3 bucket (s3://redwood-compliance-evidence/) with per-audit subfolders (e.g., SOC2-2027).
- Evidence types: configuration snapshots, access attestation emails, signed manifests for log retention/deletion, KMS key rotation logs, penetration test reports, policy documents, training records.

Evidence collection procedure (numbered):
1. Auditor request received by GRC owner (ticketed).
2. Security identifies required artifacts and maps to canonical locations.
3. Service owners produce service-specific attestations and copy artifacts to evidence bucket.
4. Security performs integrity check and stamps the evidence with a signed manifest (SHA256 + timestamp).
5. GRC packages evidence and uploads an audit binder to the auditor portal.

Retention and evidence lifecycle:
- Audit artifacts are retained according to contractual and regulatory requirements: typical minimum 3 years; critical artifacts 7 years.
- Evidence bucket uses object-lock and immutability windows matching retention policy.

7) Risk and exception process
When an exception is required (e.g., legacy service requires long-lived keys), follow this process:
1. Submit an Exception Request (Jira) with risk assessment, compensating controls, and time-bound justification (max 90 days).
2. Security reviews and either approves with compensations or rejects. High-risk exceptions require CISO and legal approval.
3. Approved exceptions are tracked in the Exceptions Register (maintained by security) and auto-expire; owners must submit renewal or close the exception at expiry.

Required compensating controls examples:
- Extra monitoring and alerts for the asset.
- Shorter credential lifetimes than default.
- Additional multi-party approval for critical actions.

Audit & reporting cadence:
- Quarterly compliance review (security + GRC + service owners).
- Annual external SOC2/ISO audit with pre-audit evidence readiness checks 60 days prior.

Appendices
A. Key service references and links:
- Identity: Okta (SSO/SCIM) — internal admin console link: https://okta.redwood.internal
- Secrets: HashiCorp Vault — https://vault.redwood.internal
- Logging: Splunk / Datadog dashboards — links maintained in the dashboard index page.
- Evidence store: s3://redwood-compliance-evidence/ (read-only to auditors)
- Incident bucket: s3://redwood-incidents/<incident-id>/

B. Runbooks and templates (quick links) — copy to incident ticket or audit binder:
- Access provisioning checklist: /internal/runbooks/access-provisioning.md
- Data deletion runbook: /internal/runbooks/data-deletion.md
- Incident evidence capture template: /internal/runbooks/incident-evidence-template.md
- Exception request template: /internal/templates/exception-request.md

C. Contact matrix (who to page by incident type):
- Security incident / suspected compromise: security-oncall@redwood.team -> PagerDuty (security-oncall)
- PII exposure: Privacy & Legal + CISO
- Operational outage affecting customers: eng-sre-oncall + product-support

D. Example exception (illustrative):
- Service: legacy-transformer-ingest
- Requested exception: allow long-lived AWS keys for a legacy CI runner
- Mitigations: restricted network, additional logging, daily credential integrity checks, expiration in 60 days
- Approval: Security (approved), CISO (approved), Legal (notified)

Revision history:
- 2026-10-15: Initial draft (Priya Nair)
- 2027-02-20: Added regional key guidance and evidence bucket structure (Ethan Park)
- 2027-11-05: Updated retention matrix and incident evidence chain-of-custody (Priya Nair)

If you are a service owner or auditor and need a packaged evidence set or runbook copy, open a request ticket with tag COMPLIANCE-EVIDENCE and include the desired audit window and customer/contract IDs.

End of document.
